item.title: AI-led services to create $100-200 billion net opportunity by 2030: BCG
item.description: BCG says AI-led services could create a $100-200 billion net market opportunity by 2030, but technology firms must upskill existing staff to deliver AI solutions at scale ...
item.dc:creator: Udisha Srivastav
item.content:encoded: Artificial intelligence (AI)-led services could create a net new market opportunity of $100-200 billion by 2030, but technology services firms risk missing out unless they build the capabilities needed to deliver AI solutions at scale, according to a new report by Boston Consulting Group (BCG). The report, titled The Talent Is Already on Your Payroll. The Clock Isn’t, argues that the primary constraint for technology services firms is not the availability of AI talent, but their ability to identify, upskill and deploy existing employees in roles involving the development and operation of AI-powered solutions. The global services market is projected to expand from $1.6-1.7 trillion in 2025 to $2.2-2.4 trillion by 2030. AI-led services are expected to contribute $300-400 billion to this growth, driven by the development and deployment of agentic AI solutions, the expansion of work that can be outsourced, and demand for human oversight and governance. However, AI-led efficiencies are also expected to reduce existing services revenue by around $200 billion, leaving a net opportunity of $100-200 billion, the report said. The findings are based on an analysis of more than 2,500 AI-tagged job postings and over 50,000 professional profiles across more than 15 firms, alongside BCG’s proprietary skills database. BCG’s analysis highlights a significant difference between technology services firms and AI-native companies in the composition of their AI workforces. Applied AI, which involves building, deploying and running AI-native and agentic solutions in production, accounts for only 10-15 per cent of the AI-tagged workforce at technology services firms. In comparison, it represents 90-95 per cent of the AI workforce at AI-native firms. The remaining 85-90 per cent of the AI-tagged workforce at technology services firms falls under “Infused AI”, where professionals use AI tools to improve the efficiency of existing work rather than build and operate AI-led solutions. BCG said firms that rely primarily on external hiring to fill emerging AI roles could face higher costs. Hiring for new Applied AI roles can cost up to 35 per cent more than hiring for comparable traditional technology roles.

item.title: Sunil Bharti Mittal awarded France's Legion of Honour for business ties
item.description: France's highest civilian distinction acknowledges the Bharti Enterprises chairman's longstanding role in expanding business cooperation and strategic engagement between the two countries ...
item.dc:creator: Sarjna Rai
item.content:encoded: France has honoured Sunil Bharti Mittal, founder and chairman of Bharti Enterprises, with its highest civilian distinction, the Legion of Honour, for his contribution to strengthening economic ties between India and France and his achievements in telecommunications and satellite communications. French Ambassador to India Thierry Mathou conferred the insignia of Chevalier de l'Ordre national de la Légion d'honneur, or Knight of the National Order of the Legion of Honour, on Mittal during a ceremony at the Residence of France on October 28. The honour recognises Mittal's role in promoting Indo-French business relations through strategic partnerships, investments and collaboration in digital infrastructure and satellite communications. Addressing the gathering, Ambassador Mathou highlighted Mittal's associations with French multinational insurance group AXA and telecommunications equipment maker Alcatel-Lucent. He also acknowledged Mittal's investment in Eutelsat, the French satellite operator, which supports France's ambition to strengthen its strategic independence in space communications. Mathou said the award reflected France's appreciation for Mittal's longstanding commitment to deepening bilateral economic ties. Accepting the award, Mittal said he was humbled by the recognition. He traced his association with France to 1992, when Compagnie Générale des Eaux partnered with Bharti to introduce mobile telephony in India. His engagement continues through his role as vice-chairman of Eutelsat. The recognition comes as India and France deepen cooperation in space and digital technology under their Special Global Strategic Partnership, with telecommunications and satellite communications emerging as important areas of collaboration.

item.title: Why Microsoft thinks most employees will reject its voluntary exit offer
item.description: Microsoft has opened a voluntary exit offer for around 60,000 employees across four countries, but CFO Amy Hood expects few eligible staff to accept, citing growth opportunities ...
item.dc:creator: Rimjhim Singh
item.content:encoded: Microsoft Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Amy Hood has said she expects “very few people” to accept the company’s voluntary exit offer, which is available to around 60,000 employees across four countries. Microsoft on Monday introduced a voluntary exit scheme for eligible employees in India, the US, the UK and Canada, offering financial assistance and career-planning support to those who choose to leave the company. According to a Business Insider report, Hood said the company believes most eligible employees will choose to stay because of growth opportunities within Microsoft. The programme is part of Microsoft’s efforts to reshape its workforce while continuing to invest heavily in artificial intelligence (AI). Why does Amy Hood expect few employees to accept the offer? In an internal memo seen by Business Insider, Hood addressed questions from employees about the purpose of the buyout programme. “I know there have been some questions on the rationale behind the voluntary exit offer that we announced this week,” Hood wrote in the memo. She said the programme was designed to give employees the option to leave on their own terms. “Our intent is to offer employees agency if they choose to leave the company on their own terms. We expect very few people to select this offer because of the growth opportunities here at Microsoft,” Hood added, as quoted by the report. Who can apply for Microsoft’s voluntary exit offer? Microsoft Chief People Officer Amy Coleman shared details of the programme in a separate memo sent to employees on Monday. “The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” Coleman wrote. The offer is available to eligible employees at internal level 70 or below in the US, Canada, India and the UK. However, some sales teams, engineering roles and certain corporate functions are not included. Microsoft said around 60,000 employees qualify for the programme. The package is expected to be similar to its standard severance benefits. Employees have until early December to decide whether to accept the offer. Those who opt in are expected to leave by the end of the year. How much could employees receive? The severance amount will depend on an employee’s role and years of service. According to the report, Microsoft’s severance package during layoffs earlier this year included at least 60 days of base pay, with employees remaining on the payroll during that period. Depending on seniority and length of service, many employees were eligible for up to 39 weeks of base pay. Offer letters reviewed by Business Insider showed that employees at internal levels 64 and below received one week of base pay for every six months of service. Those at levels 65 to 67 were offered two weeks of base pay for every six months of service. Why is Microsoft offering voluntary exits? The voluntary exit programme comes as Microsoft continues to spend billions of dollars on AI infrastructure while reducing its workforce. By allowing eligible employees to leave voluntarily, the company is offering an alternative to compulsory layoffs. The move could help Microsoft lower staffing costs while giving employees more control over their next career decision. Hood’s comments also indicate that Microsoft expects most employees to stay with the company despite the offer, citing future opportunities within the business. What happened in Microsoft’s earlier voluntary retirement programme? Earlier this year, Microsoft introduced a voluntary retirement scheme for senior employees at director level and below. In July, the company said more than 30 per cent of the 8,750 employees eligible for the programme had chosen to take part. That same month, Microsoft announced plans to cut 4,800 jobs, equivalent to about 2.1 per cent of its global workforce. The cuts affected several teams, including a significant number of employees in its Xbox gaming business.

item.title: Australia sees gains in contest with China for Pacific's 'great game'
item.description: Pacific Island Affairs Minister Pat Conroy said Canberra must deliver on regional commitments to remain the partner of choice, citing treaties and new alliances as key achievements ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By James Mayger Australia’s “permanent contest” with China for influence in the Pacific region, a challenge compared to the 19th century’s Great Game, has made progress over the past few years, according to the official leading the charge against Beijing. “I think we’ve done pretty well,” Minister for Pacific Island Affairs Pat Conroy said in an interview. Yet Canberra now has to deliver on commitments it has made across the region if it wants to remain the partner of choice, he said, adding it’s his job to ensure “every Pacific nation that’s elevated their relationship with us sees the benefits of that.” Since taking power in 2022, the center-left government has focused its foreign and defense policies on China, rebooting ties with Beijing while also attempting to counter its growing sway across the region. Pacific island nations have been a particular focus of Canberra, which is working to undo China’s attempts to build security ties with the tiny states and replace them instead with stronger relationships with Australia, the US and New Zealand.   “We can’t rest on our laurels. It’s a permanent contest,” Conroy said late Wednesday in his office in Canberra, which is decorated with gifts from across the region gathered during his four years in the role.  “But if you think about what we’ve achieved since 2022 with the treaties with Tuvalu, with Nauru, with Fiji, PNG, Vanuatu, the two new alliances, the fact that we’re negotiating treaties right now with Solomons and with Tonga — I think this is one of the critical foreign policy achievements of the Albanese government.”  The attempt to overturn China’s pact with the Solomon Islands is emblematic of that effort.  In 2022, just prior to the Australian election that brought Conroy’s Labor party to power, the Pacific nation signed a security deal with China. Canberra has spent the past four years trying to reverse that accord and an “in principle” deal agreed last month with the Solomons’ new, Australia-friendly leader, is seen as a vindication of that effort. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Thursday he would meet with his Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale next week at an international meeting, along with the leaders of Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Tuvalu and Nauru. While Australia is the largest development partner for Pacific island nations, according to the Lowy Institute in Sydney, it has failed to sufficiently promote those efforts and to emphasize the economic advantages of ties with Canberra compared with Beijing, Conroy said.   “Being very frank with you, we can do better on public diplomacy,” he said. “We’ve been focused on delivering projects that have the best value for our partner countries, rather than getting credit for it. And that’s obviously something that comes at a cost for us. So we need to get better at the public diplomacy aspect of it.” Another area where the government has sought to roll back Beijing’s influence is by reducing the presence of Chinese contractors in the construction phase of development activities across the region. “Too often, there are projects around the Indo-Pacific, but particularly in the Pacific, that are funded by countries like Australia and Japan, that because the tendering process has been flawed, and they’ve chosen the lowest bidder rather than the best quality, have gone to a state-owned enterprise of China,” Conroy said.  “Then the Chinese state-owned enterprise has branded it with their branding, and people assume China is funding the project, when it’s taxpayers of Japan or Australia,” he said. Chinese SOEs win a substantial amount of the contracts from multilateral development banks, according to Lowy, although these institutions have acknowledged complaints from Australia and others, according to Conroy. He said the World Bank is moving the fastest to change its procurement practices to prioritize quality and local content over cost.  The Asian Development Bank is also improving, but “I’d still like them to do better in terms of choosing tenderers who prioritize local content,” Conroy said. “If a project’s good enough to be in the Solomons, it’s good enough to use Solomons companies and Solomons workers rather than shipping them all in.” Australia’s drive in the Pacific has elicited some pushback from China, according to Conroy. While declining to detail the specific countermeasures Beijing has used, he reiterated that “we’re in a permanent state of contest. We expect every move we take to advance our partnerships to be tested by other countries who want to be the primary partner.”
